meta.title: Essential Travel Info — Tbilisi
meta.description: Everything a first-time visitor needs to know about traveling in Tbilisi, Georgia: currency, transport, safety, weather, apps and more.

hero.title: Essential Travel Info
hero.sub: Everything a first-time visitor needs to feel at home in Tbilisi — money, transport, safety, and the little things locals wish you knew.

firstTime.heading: First-Time Visitor Essentials
firstTime.sub: The eight things worth knowing before you land.

items.title: Currency
items.detail: Cards accepted almost everywhere. Carry small cash for markets, marshrutkas, and rural areas.

items.title: Language
items.detail: English is common in tourist areas; Russian is widely understood. A friendly “gamarjoba” (hello) goes a long way.

items.title: Time Zone
items.detail: Georgia Standard Time. No daylight saving — the clocks never change.

items.title: Emergency
items.detail: One number for police, fire, and ambulance. English-speaking operators available.

items.title: Power Plugs
items.detail: European two-pin plugs, 220V / 50Hz. Bring an adapter if you're from the US or UK.

items.title: Drinking Water
items.detail: Tbilisi tap water is clean and safe to drink. Refill your bottle from the city's fountains too.

items.title: Visa
items.detail: Citizens of ~95 countries (EU, US, UK, Canada, Australia and more) enter visa-free for up to 365 days. Confirm your own eligibility.

items.title: Best Time to Visit
items.detail: Mild temperatures, fewer crowds, and the vineyards at their best. Summer is hot; winter is cold but charming.

gettingAround.heading: Getting Around
gettingAround.sub: From the airport to your last khinkali — how to move through the city.

airport.title: From Tbilisi International Airport (TBS)
points: The airport sits about 17 km southeast of the center — roughly 20–30 minutes by car.
Bus 337 runs between the airport and Freedom Square day and night for a flat fare, paid with a Metromoney card or contactless bank card.
The train to Tbilisi Central runs only a few times a day — check the schedule before relying on it.
For a taxi, order through the Bolt app rather than accepting rides from drivers who approach you inside the terminal.

transit.title: Metro, Bus & Marshrutka
points: The metro has two lines and is the fastest way across the center. Trains run roughly 06:00–24:00.
City buses are modern, air-conditioned, and tracked live in the TTC / Google Maps apps.
Marshrutkas (minibuses) cover routes buses don't — pay the driver and tell them where to stop.
One flat fare covers 90 minutes of transfers across metro, bus, and marshrutka when you tap the same card.

taxi.title: Taxis & Ride-hailing
points: Bolt is the default ride-hailing app — cheap, reliable, and cashless. Yandex Go also works.
Always prefer an app so the fare is fixed up front and you avoid haggling.
Street taxis rarely use meters; agree the price before getting in if you must take one.
Most short rides across the center cost only a few lari.

walking.title: On Foot
points: The Old Town, Sololaki, and Rustaveli Avenue are best explored on foot.
Wear comfortable shoes — cobblestones and steep lanes are part of the charm.
The aerial cableway from Rike Park up to Narikala Fortress is a scenic shortcut worth taking.
Streets are well-lit and walkable in the center late into the evening.

card.title: The Metromoney Card
points: Buy a rechargeable Metromoney card at any metro station for a small deposit.
One card can pay for several people — just tap once per person.
It works on the metro, city buses, marshrutkas, and the Rike–Narikala cableway.
Contactless bank cards and Apple/Google Pay also work directly on buses and the metro.

safety.heading: Safety
safety.sub: Tbilisi is one of the safest capitals in the region.
safety.intro: Violent crime against tourists is rare, and locals are famously hospitable. A little everyday awareness is all you need.
tips: Petty theft is uncommon but watch your belongings in crowded markets and on packed transit.
Traffic can be assertive — cross at marked crossings and don't assume cars will stop.
Tap water is safe, but stick to bottled water on trips into the mountains.
Solo travelers, including women, generally report feeling safe day and night in the center.
Save the emergency number 112 and your accommodation's address in Georgian.

etiquette.heading: Local Rules & Etiquette
etiquette.sub: Small courtesies that Georgians deeply appreciate.
dos: Accept hospitality warmly — being offered food, wine, or a toast is a genuine honor.
Dress modestly when visiting churches — cover shoulders and knees; women may cover their heads.
Let the tamada (toastmaster) lead the toasts at a supra feast.
donts: Don't refuse a toast outright at the table — sip if you can't drink a full glass.
Don't discuss politics with strangers unless invited; topics like the 2008 conflict are sensitive.
Don't photograph people, especially in rural areas, without a smile and a nod first.
Don't tip excessively — rounding up or leaving 10% is plenty where service isn't included.

accessibility.heading: Accessibility
accessibility.sub: An honest picture for travelers with mobility needs.
points: The historic center's cobblestones, steep lanes, and stairs make some areas challenging for wheelchairs.
Not all metro stations have elevators; newer buses are low-floor and wheelchair-friendly.
Larger hotels and modern restaurants increasingly offer step-free access — call ahead to confirm.
Bolt lets you note accessibility needs, and drivers are generally willing to help.
Pavements can be uneven; a travel companion is helpful for the Old Town's hilliest parts.

faq.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.sub: Quick answers to what visitors ask most.

items.q: Do I need to tip in Tbilisi?
items.a: Tipping isn't mandatory. Many restaurants add a 10% service charge; if not, rounding up or leaving 10% is a kind gesture.

items.q: Can I drink the tap water?
items.a: Yes. Tbilisi's tap water is clean and safe to drink straight from the tap.

items.q: Is Tbilisi expensive?
items.a: It's very affordable by European standards. A hearty meal, a taxi across town, or a metro ride each cost only a few lari.

items.q: Do people speak English?
items.a: In tourist areas, hotels, and among younger people, yes. Learning a few Georgian words is warmly welcomed everywhere.

items.q: Is it safe for solo and women travelers?
items.a: Generally very safe. Most solo travelers, including women, feel comfortable exploring the center day and night with normal awareness.

items.q: How do I pay for public transport?
items.a: Tap a Metromoney card or a contactless bank card. One fare covers 90 minutes of transfers across metro, bus, and marshrutka.

items.q: What's the best way to get from the airport?
items.a: Order a Bolt for door-to-door convenience, or take bus 337 to Freedom Square for a flat fare.

faq.heading: Food & Drink FAQs
faq.sub: What travelers ask before eating out in Tbilisi.

items.q: What is the best area to eat in Tbilisi?
items.a: Vera and Old Town have the highest concentration of well-reviewed restaurants and cafés, while Marjanishvili and Fabrika are best for wine bars and nightlife.

items.q: What food is Tbilisi famous for?
items.a: Khinkali (soup dumplings), khachapuri (cheese bread), and natural Georgian wine are the essentials — most restaurants on this list serve all three.

items.q: Is Tbilisi nightlife good?
items.a: Yes — Tbilisi has a well-known techno and rooftop bar scene, especially around Marjanishvili and Fabrika, alongside more relaxed wine bars in Old Town.

items.q: Do restaurants in Tbilisi accept cards?
items.a: Cards are accepted almost everywhere in the city center, though smaller wine bars and food halls may prefer cash.

faq.heading: Attractions FAQs
faq.sub: Common questions about sightseeing in Tbilisi.

items.q: What are the must-see attractions in Tbilisi?
items.a: Narikala Fortress, the Old Town sulphur baths, Rike Park, and the Bridge of Peace are the most-visited sights, alongside the National Museum and Dry Bridge Market.

items.q: How many days do you need to see Tbilisi's main attractions?
items.a: 2-3 days covers the core Old Town sights comfortably; add a day for museums and neighborhood walks if you want a deeper visit.

items.q: Is Tbilisi walkable?
items.a: Yes, the Old Town and central neighborhoods are very walkable, though the cable car and metro help cover longer distances quickly.

faq.heading: Activities FAQs
faq.sub: What travelers ask about Tbilisi tours and activities.

items.q: What is the most popular activity in Tbilisi?
items.a: The Old Town walking tour and Georgian wine & food tasting are the two most-booked experiences, alongside sulphur bath visits.

items.q: Are there boat tours in Tbilisi?
items.a: Yes, short Mtkvari river boat rides are available near the Old Town and Rike Park, popular for photos of the Peace Bridge and Narikala Fortress.

items.q: Do I need to book city tours in advance?
items.a: Popular tours and wine tastings can fill up in summer — booking 1-2 days ahead is recommended.

faq.heading: Events FAQs
faq.sub: Common questions about events in Tbilisi.

items.q: What events happen in Tbilisi in summer?
items.a: Tbilisi Open Air and the Georgian Wine Festival are the two biggest summer events, both drawing large local and international crowds.

items.q: Where can I find live music in Tbilisi?
items.a: Fabrika, Mtkvari riverbank venues, and dedicated festival grounds host most of the city's live music events throughout the year.

items.q: Do Tbilisi festivals sell out?
items.a: Major festivals like Tbilisi Open Air can sell out — buying tickets in advance online is recommended.
